newsitem.title: FRANCE: France reasonably satisfied with Amsterdam summit.
newsitem.headline: France reasonably satisfied with Amsterdam summit.

text.p: French leaders expressed muted satisfaction on Wednesday with a European Union summit that produced a watered-down treaty and papered over Franco-German differences on jobs and budget austerity.

Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who came to power this month after ousting the centre-right in an upset election, said he was "reasonably" satisfied with the Amsterdam summit that ended early on Wednesday.

Earlier in Amsterdam, conservative President Jacques Chirac called the summit a "reasonable step" paving the way to EU expansion into Eastern Europe and enabling the EU to push ahead with plans for a single European currency from 1999.

Jospin said he was pleased with the first part of the summit that approved a plan demanded by France to bolster jobs and growth as well as a stability pact championed by Germany to limit budget deficits from 1999.

He said he was "a little less" content with the second half of the summit, during which the EU cobbled together a new pact to update the Maastricht Treaty on European construction, but only after stripping out some key points of dispute.
Government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said Jospin had told a cabinet meeting that France had not intended to cause a crisis at Amsterdam. "The crisis was clearly avoided," she said.

The new treaty, after 15 months of negotiations, includes an employment chapter and deeper cooperation on asylum, immigration and crime-busting, but puts off changes to the balance of power in the bloc until new members join early next century.

The French daily Le Monde said the summit had failed in its ambitions to reform EU institutions. A cartoon showed EU leaders with a diplomat commenting: "No big decisions! Nothing dropped! Maybe that's the stability pact!"
Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine, speaking after a cabinet meeting, called the deal a "reasonable compromise" and said the summit provided a springboard for an EU assault on unemployment.

Junior Minister for European Affairs Pierre Moscovici, rebuked by Jospin on Tuesday for hinting France was not fully committed to the euro single currency, said: "France wants to take part in the euro."
Vedrine said it was getting harder to keep the Franco-German duo at the heart of the European Union in step, but he played down strains at Amsterdam.

"It's less automatic to find convergence...it's a bit more laborious," Vedrine told Europe 1 radio hours after the Amsterdam summit ended. "Simply, the problems are getting more complicated, for each European country it's more complicated than before to find convergence with any other.
"France is evolving, it has its problems and its social demands, its new political situation."
The summit was a first EU test of Jospin's awkward left-right power-sharing with Chirac.
"Germany is having problems it did not have before. Chancellor (Helmut) Kohl perhaps does not have the same margin for manoeuvre that he had for years," Vedrine said.
"However, his commitment to Europe and to the euro remains completely central," he said.
Kohl's coalition has been closer to collapse than ever in its 14-year history as its members clash over how to plug gaps in the budget to qualify Germany for monetary union in 1999.
Jospin had thrown plans for the summit into confusion last week by demanding more time to study the budget stability pact. In the end the pact was approved unchanged.
